title: Craving Ice: Why You Want to Chew Ice, When to Worry and the Blood Tests That Check
summary: Why do I crave ice? See how low iron explains most ice cravings, when to worry, whether chewing ice hurts your teeth, and which blood tests check it.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**A strong, lasting urge to chew or eat ice is a recognized sign of low iron.** The medical name is pagophagia, and it is a form of pica, the pattern of eating things that are not food \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001538.htm) \]. A desire to eat ice is a listed symptom of iron deficiency anemia \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \], and a 2025 review in JAMA lists pica among the symptoms of iron deficiency with or without anemia \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \].


**The blood tests that check an ice craving are a ferritin test, a complete blood count (CBC) and iron studies** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]\[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. Ferritin shows how much iron your body has stored, the CBC shows whether you have anemia, and iron studies show how much iron is moving in your blood \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \]. The JAMA review says testing for iron deficiency is indicated when someone has symptoms such as tiredness, pica or restless legs \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. Low iron also has a cause, such as heavy periods, pregnancy, frequent blood donation, celiac disease or bleeding in the gut, and that cause needs finding too \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]\[[7](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/causes) \].


## When to see a doctor about craving ice


**Some symptoms that come with an ice craving should not wait for a routine blood test.** Get care promptly if you have:


- blood in your stool, or stool that is black and tar-like, which can be a sign of bleeding in the gut \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \];
- chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness or fainting, which serious anemia can cause \[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]\[[8](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/symptoms) \];
- periods so heavy that you soak through one or more pads or tampons every hour for several hours in a row, or bleeding that lasts more than 7 days \[[9](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/heavy-menstrual-bleeding) \];
- an urge to eat things other than ice, such as dirt, clay or paint chips, which can cause blockages in the stomach, infections or lead poisoning \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001538.htm) \].


An ice craving on its own, without these signs, is still worth a ferritin test and a CBC. It is not an emergency, but it is one of the more specific clues to low iron \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \].


## Why low iron may cause ice cravings


**No one knows for sure why low iron makes people crave ice.** The link itself is well described: pica, including ice eating, is a listed symptom of iron deficiency \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]\[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. The mechanism behind it is not established.


One idea comes from a 2025 review of the research on pagophagia \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40325012/) \]. In one study it describes, people with iron deficiency did worse on an attention test, and eating ice improved their response time compared with drinking lukewarm water. Cold in the mouth is known to raise blood flow to the brain, so the authors suggest ice may help attention by raising blood flow or delivering more oxygen to the brain \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40325012/) \]. That is a hypothesis that still needs more research, not a proven explanation \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40325012/) \].


How common is it? The JAMA review puts pica at 40% to 50% of people with iron deficiency \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. In a study of 41 men with iron deficiency anemia, 14 (34%) had pagophagia \[[11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30986649/) \]. These figures come from people already diagnosed, so they say how often the craving shows up with low iron, not how often a craving means low iron.


Iron deficiency happens in stages. Iron stores fall first, and anemia, a low hemoglobin, comes later \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. That is why a[ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) test matters even when a past CBC was normal. For the other signs of the early stage, see[symptoms of low ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-ferritin) and[symptoms of low iron](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-iron) .


## Other causes of craving ice


**Low iron is the cause most closely linked to ice craving, but it is not the only one.** The sources describe these:


- **Pregnancy.** In women, pica is most often seen during pregnancy \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335275/) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001538.htm) \]. Pregnancy also raises iron needs, so the two often overlap \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]\[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \].
- **Low zinc.** MedlinePlus notes that a lack of certain nutrients, such as iron and zinc, may trigger the unusual cravings of pica \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001538.htm) \].
- **Pica as an eating disorder.** Pica can occur on its own, and sometimes alongside obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) or other mental health conditions \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335275/) \]. To count as pica, the eating has to last at least a month \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335275/) \].
- **Cultural practice.** In some parts of the world, eating certain non-food substances is culturally accepted \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335275/) \].


Wanting a cold drink or crunching an occasional ice cube on a hot day is not pica. What points to a medical cause is an urge that is strong, lasts weeks, and has you chewing ice most days. For how ice fits with other cravings, see[why do I crave salt](https://mitohealth.com/blog/salt-cravings) and[cravings in women](https://mitohealth.com/symptoms/cravings-in-women) .


## Is eating ice bad for you and your teeth?


**Ice is frozen water, so the main direct risk the sources describe is to your teeth.** The American Dental Association lists chewing ice among the habits that damage teeth \[[14](https://www.mouthhealthy.org/bad-habits-for-dental-health) \]. Tooth enamel and ice are both crystals, and when two crystals are pushed together one breaks. Most of the time it is the ice, but sometimes it is the tooth or a filling \[[14](https://www.mouthhealthy.org/bad-habits-for-dental-health) \]. The ADA suggests drinking chilled drinks without ice, or using a straw so you are not tempted \[[14](https://www.mouthhealthy.org/bad-habits-for-dental-health) \].


The bigger concern is what the craving may be telling you. If it comes from low iron, chewing less ice does not fix the iron. Low iron left untreated can lead to heart problems and infections \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \], and iron deficiency anemia makes it harder to work, exercise and control your body temperature \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \].


**Does ice count as water?** Yes. Melted ice counts toward your fluid intake like any other water, although a glass of ice holds less water than a glass of water because of the air between the cubes.


## Which blood tests check an ice craving


**A ferritin test, a CBC and iron studies together show whether low iron is behind the craving, and how far it has gone** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \]. Each one answers a different question:


Test What it measures What points to low iron


[Ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) How much iron your body has stored \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \] A low result. The JAMA review uses a ferritin typically below 30 ng/mL, in people without inflammatory conditions \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]


Complete blood count (CBC) Red blood cells,[hemoglobin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hemoglobin) , hematocrit and red cell size \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \] Low hemoglobin means anemia. With iron deficiency, red cells become smaller and carry less hemoglobin, which shows as a low[MCV](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/mcv) \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]


Iron studies: serum[iron](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/iron) ,[TIBC](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/tibc) and iron saturation How much iron is in the blood and how well it binds to transferrin, the protein that carries it \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \] An iron saturation (transferrin saturation) below 20% \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]


Reticulocyte count Young red blood cells, newly released by the bone marrow Part of the blood count used to diagnose iron deficiency anemia \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]


**The JAMA review’s ferritin cutoff applies to people without inflammatory conditions, and iron saturation is the second way it diagnoses iron deficiency** \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. That is one reason a full set of iron studies is more informative than ferritin alone. For what your number means, see[ferritin levels](https://mitohealth.com/guide/ferritin-level) and[symptoms of low iron saturation](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-iron-saturation) . For how the CBC and iron tests fit together, see[the anemia test guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/anemia-test) .


Timing matters for iron studies. The amount of iron in your blood varies through the day and may be higher in the morning \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \], and a provider may ask you to fast before a ferritin test, which is usually done in the morning \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \].

## Why you might be low on iron


**Finding low iron is the start, not the end, because iron deficiency always has a cause.** The JAMA review names bleeding (menstrual or from the gut), poor absorption, too little iron in the diet and pregnancy as the most common causes, and says the cause should be identified and treated \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]. These are the groups the sources name:


- **Heavy periods.** Blood loss from heavy periods can lead to iron deficiency anemia \[[9](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/heavy-menstrual-bleeding) \]. NHLBI advises seeing a doctor if you need to change a pad or tampon after less than 2 hours, or pass clots the size of a quarter or larger \[[7](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/causes) \].
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding.** Both raise the amount of iron the body needs \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]\[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]. In high-income countries, iron deficiency affects up to 84% of pregnant women in the third trimester \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \].
- **Frequent blood donation.** Frequent blood donors are among the groups most likely to have trouble getting enough iron \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/iron-tests/) \], and donating blood often is a listed risk factor for anemia \[[7](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/causes) \].
- **Bleeding in the gut.** Bleeding from an ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease or colon cancer, and regular use of aspirin or anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and naproxen, can all cause iron loss \[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]\[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \]. In the study of men with iron deficiency anemia, 36 of 41 (88%) had bleeding in the gut \[[11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30986649/) \]. That is why finding low iron can lead to tests that look for blood loss, such as a colonoscopy, a stool test for blood or an upper endoscopy \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \].
- **Celiac disease and other absorption problems.** Celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, H. pylori infection and stomach or weight loss surgery can all reduce how much iron the gut absorbs \[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]\[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \].
- **Diet.** People who do not eat meat, poultry or seafood can run low on iron, so a plant-based diet is worth considering too \[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]\[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000584.htm) \].
- **Endurance sports.** Endurance athletes can lose iron through the gut and through the breakdown of red blood cells \[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \].


Low iron also causes symptoms beyond the craving, including tiredness, weakness, trouble concentrating, restless legs and cold hands and feet \[[3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159291/) \]\[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]\[[13](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-Consumer/) \]. For aches that come with anemia, see[can anemia cause body aches](https://mitohealth.com/blog/can-anemia-cause-body-aches-understanding-the-link-to-muscle-and-joint-pain) . For twitches and cramps, which have their own set of blood tests, see[muscle twitching](https://mitohealth.com/blog/muscle-twitching) .


## After treatment: does the ice craving go away?


**Ice cravings caused by low iron are treated by replacing the iron, and the craving is expected to fade as iron recovers.** A 2025 review describes pagophagia as caused by iron deficiency and treated with iron replacement \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40325012/) \]. In the study of 41 men whose iron deficiency anemia resolved after iron replacement, the 14 who craved ice also saw the craving go away \[[11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30986649/) \].


Restoring iron takes time. NHLBI says it often takes three to six months to restore iron levels with iron pills \[[15](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]. That is why a ferritin recheck is useful: a ferritin test can show how well treatment is working \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \], and a craving that fades is a good sign but not proof that stores are full.


Test before you start iron on your own. Iron supplements are generally not given to people who do not have iron deficiency anemia, because too much iron can damage organs \[[16](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/treatment) \]. For what helps ferritin rise once you know it is low, see[raising ferritin levels](https://mitohealth.com/blog/raising-ferritin-levels-why-it-matters-and-how-to-do-it-right) .


If the craving does not fade once your iron is back in range, or your iron results were normal from the start, tell your clinician. The other causes of pica, including low zinc and pica as an eating disorder, are then worth looking at \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001538.htm) \]\[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335275/) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### Is craving ice a sign of anemia?


It can be. A desire to eat ice or other non-food things is a listed symptom of iron deficiency anemia, and a review in JAMA lists pica among the symptoms of iron deficiency both with and without anemia. That means ferritin can be low while hemoglobin is still normal. A ferritin test checks your iron stores, and a complete blood count (CBC) shows whether anemia is present.


### Is chewing ice bad for your teeth?


Yes, it can be. The American Dental Association explains that tooth enamel and ice are both crystals, and when they are pushed together one breaks. Most of the time it is the ice, but sometimes it is the tooth or a filling. The ADA suggests drinking chilled drinks without ice, or using a straw so you are not tempted to chew.


### Does eating ice count as drinking water?


Yes. Ice is frozen water, so the water it melts into counts toward your fluid intake like any other water. A glass of ice holds less water than the same glass filled with water, because of the air between the cubes. Letting ice melt in a drink gives you the same water without the risk to your teeth that comes with chewing it.


### What is pagophagia?


Pagophagia is the medical name for compulsively eating or chewing ice. It is a form of pica, the pattern of eating things that are not food, such as ice, clay, dirt or paper. Iron deficiency is the cause most often linked to it, and in women pica is most often seen during pregnancy. A study of men with iron deficiency anemia found that about a third of them had pagophagia.


### Why do I crave ice when I am pregnant?


Pregnancy raises the amount of iron the body needs, and pica, including ice eating, is most often seen in women during pregnancy. In high-income countries, iron deficiency affects up to 84% of pregnant women in the third trimester, according to a JAMA review. A ferritin test and a complete blood count (CBC) check whether low iron is behind the craving.
